subject: abstracted autodiff on the road to RM-HMC

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: abstracted autodiff on the road to RM-HMC
parts:
I just pushed a reasonably complete agrad/autodiff.hpp
file to the fvar branch (fvar is where Peter Li and I
have been working on forward-mode auto-dif).

I implemented the design I sketched in the Stan meeting
last week, which lets users of C++ get at autodiff without
having to look at the autodiff types themselves. The
basic rundown of operations is:

single input, single output
-- derivative (& function value)

multiple input, single output
-- partial derivative (& function value)
-- gradient (& function value)
-- Hessian (& function val, gradient)
-- gradient-vector dot product (& function val)
-- Hessian times vector (& function val)
-- gradient of trace of matrix times Hessian

multiple input, multiple output
-- Jacobian (& function val)

Despite the seeming complexity, gradient-vector dot
product is just a directional derivative and can be done
using a single forward-mode autodiff pass. The Hessian
times vector takes O(N) time, not O(N^2). The graiden
of trace of matrix times Hessian takes O(N^2) time, not
O(N^3).

Here's an example of how they look from the C++ API:

template <typename F>
void
hessian_times_vector(const F& f,
const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& v,
double& fx,
Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& Hv);

The typename F needs to be filled in with a functor that
defines an operator on Eigen vectors returning a scalar with the
type of the scalars and vector type templated out:

struct fun1 {
template <typename T>
inline
T operator()(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
return x(0) * x(0) * x(1)
+ 3.0 * x(1) * x(1);
}
};

Then you can just define an instance of the functor:

fun1 f;

and the arguments x and v,

Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> x = ...;
Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> v = ...;

and then set up locals to store the results into

double fx;
Matrix<double,Dynamic,1> Hv;

and then call the function

hessian_times_vector(f,x,v,fx,Hv);

and now Hv now holds hessian times vector and fx the value.

So far, we can only define functions using underlying library
functions that are implemented for forward autodiff variables fvar.
But we'll work on getting this rounded out to all of the
Stan library functions. (I'm hoping we can just further template out
the probability functions, which will only leave the matrix functions.)

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] abstracted autodiff on the road to RM-HMC
parts:
On 2/25/13 4:39 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Yeah, this is totally awesome! I don't suppose that the tr(AH) is
> implemented in a way that makes it O(N) when A is diagonal (e.g., if
> it's the identity matrix)?

I'll have to think about this for a bit longer.
It's a second-order directional derivative,

tr(A*H) = SUM_n A[n,n] * d^2/dx[n]^2 f(x)

but I'm not sure I can just do that the same way
as a first-order directional derivative (initialize
the second order derivative for x[n] to A[n,n] instead
of 1). Let me get some paper out and get back to you.

What I've implemented so far is just what Michael needed
for RM-HMC, which is

grad tr(M*H).

I could also pull out a more efficient O(N^2)
version of tr(M*H) alone that skips the last backward
pass (and thus has double types instead of agrad::var
reverse-mode types).

And when I'm writing O(N^2), it's really proportional
to O(N) function evals, where I'm assuming each of those
is O(N). If the log probability function is more intense,
as when it contains nasty O(N^3) matrix ops, then it's
more complex. I should write this some other way,
like O(N * f(N)), where f is the order of a log prob
function eval for inputs of size N.

- Bob
